newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Inquiry mulls Australia guarantee on deposits.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Inquiry mulls Australia guarantee on deposits.

text.p: The Wallis Inquiry into Australia's financial system is considering whether laws should be changed to make clear that the government no longer guarantees money in bank deposit accounts.

The Inquiry, set up by the government and headed by prominent businessman Stan Wallis, said in its interim discussion paper released on Thursday it would also look at finding ways of making explicit those guarantees that do exist.
"Most people assume that their deposits are completely safe under all circumstances," the Inquiry said.

"Indeed, because of depositor priority and supervision arrangements (where the Reserve Bank of Australia monitors the strength of the system and works to prevent failures), this is a reasonable assumption under all but the most extraordinary circumstances," it said.
"However, there is no government guarantee of deposits and no insurance scheme to back them in the event of extraordinary failure," the paper said.

The Inquiry said it would look at amending the laws for "depositor protection to make clear that there is no government guarantee in any area of the financial system or, alternatively, establishing means for making any guarantees and their funding explicit."

The Inquiry, which will make its recommendations in a report to the government before the end of March 1997, said that the government had guaranteed deposits in state and government-owned banks in the past. But these banks have since been sold off and these explicit guarantees are being phased out.
Under the 1959 Banking Act, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) is empowered to protect depositors' funds and has in the past arranged mergers and takeovers to stop a bank from failing.
The RBA also has the power to take control of a bank if it cannot be sold or merged. If it still fails then depositors funds rank ahead of the bank's creditor's, including the RBA.
In effect any funds pumped into the failing bank by the RBA pass to the depositor. This in effect means the government can contribute to the depositor through lost RBA profits.
But nowhere in the current laws is a government or RBA guarantee that all depositors' funds would be repaid.
"The RBA favoured amendments to the act to clarify its powers and to make it clear tha depositor protection does not meant an official guarantee of deposits," the paper said.
